propositions.text: The claimant is XXXXXXXXXXX, a Chinese citizen claiming refugee protection under IRPA sections 96 and 97(1).
propositions.quote: This is the decision in the claim of, XXXXXXXXXXX, who claims to be a citizen of China and who is claiming refugee protection pursuant to Section 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

propositions.text: The decision is edited for syntax, grammar, and includes references to case law and documentary evidence as necessary.
propositions.quote: Edited for syntax and grammar, as well as, I will add references to applicable case law and any other documentary evidence as may be necessary.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the claimant is a Chinese citizen seeking refugee protection under IRPA and that the decision is edited for clarity and references.

propositions.text: The claimant befriended two Taiwanese preachers in 2009 and allowed them to use his grandfather's home for underground church services.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges that in 2009, he became friends with two Taiwanese preachers who introduced him to Christianity...allowed his friends to use his grandfather's vacant home as a site where they could preach the gospel and hold underground church services.

propositions.text: The claimant assisted the preachers by interpreting and became a Christian during this time.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges that he assisted the preachers by interpreting on their behalf and that in the course of doing so he became a Christian.

propositions.text: The village committee head asked the preachers to register the church, but they refused.
propositions.quote: In XXXX 2009, the head of the village committee, asked the preachers to register the church, however they refused.

propositions.text: The church was raided by the Public Security Bureau; 18 congregants and two preachers were arrested and bibles seized.
propositions.quote: On XXXX, 2009, the church was raided by members of the Public Security Bureau. All 18 congregants were arrested along with the two preachers. In addition all of the bibles were seized.

propositions.text: The claimant went into hiding after the raid and learned the Public Security Bureau sought him at home.
propositions.quote: Upon hearing this, the claimant went into hiding. He subsequently learned that the Public Security Bureau went to his home looking for him.

propositions.text: Fearing arrest, the claimant used a smuggler to leave China for Canada and filed a refugee claim.
propositions.quote: Fearing he would be arrested the claimant used the services of a smuggler to leave China for Canada where he filed a refugee protection claim.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges he became a Christian in 2009, helped Taiwanese preachers, the church was raided, he hid, and fled China fearing arrest.

propositions.text: The claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection on a balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: I find on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection; the reasons are as follows.

propositions.text: The key issue is the credibility of the claimant's testimony and documentary evidence regarding his Christian identity.
propositions.quote: The determinative issue in this claim is the credibility of the claimant's oral testimony and documentary evidence in regard to his identity as a Christian.

propositions.text: The claimant was not a credible witness regarding his Christian identity.
propositions.quote: In this regard, I find that the claimant was not a credible witness.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant not credible and not a refugee or person in need of protection, focusing on his Christian identity credibility.

propositions.text: The claimant alleges 18 church members were arrested, held six months, fined 5,000 Yuan, and pastors deported.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges that 18 of his fellow church members were arrested and that each was held for a period of six months and fined 5,000 Yuan. The claimant also alleges that the two pastors were subsequently deported.

propositions.text: The claimant's testimony conflicts with country condition documents about Christians in Fujian province.
propositions.quote: The claimant's testimony in this regard runs counter to the country condition documents which I will discuss later in these reasons with the analysis of the situation of Christians in Fujian province.

propositions.text: A negative inference is drawn from the claimant's conflicting testimony.
propositions.quote: In this regard I draw a negative inference.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges arrests and fines of church members, but the court finds his testimony conflicts with country documents and draws a negative inference.

propositions.text: The claimant alleges the PSB visited his home nine times to arrest him, pursuing him until 2011.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges that the PSB have attended his home on nine occasions with the intent of arresting him and that they have continued to pursue him as late as XXXX of 2011.

propositions.text: The claimant submitted a Notice of Summoning allegedly left with his family after the 2009 raid.
propositions.quote: The claimant tendered a document entitled Notice of Summoning that he alleged was left with his family after the raid on XXXX, 2009.

propositions.text: There are concerns about the summons' genuineness causing doubt about the document.
propositions.quote: I have noted a number of concerns with the summons which causes me to question its genuineness.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges multiple PSB visits and submits a summons, but the court questions the summons' genuineness due to concerns.

propositions.text: Summonses are usually issued to individuals, but often left with family members who must pass it on and sign receipt.
propositions.quote: The documentary evidence regarding the issuance of a summons notes that a summons would almost always be issued to the individual rather than a household or a family member. However, it also noted that it is very common in China for the police authorities to leave the summons with family members instructing them to pass it along to the persons named on the summons. The person accepting the summons would be expected to sign an acknowledgement of receipt.

propositions.text: Although not proper procedure, leaving summons with family and signing receipt happens often when the person is hard to locate.
propositions.quote: Although this is not actually the proper procedure it happens all the time, especially in cases when a person in the summons is not easily locatable.

paragraphs.summary: Documentary evidence shows summonses usually go to individuals but often left with family who sign receipt, though not proper procedure.

propositions.text: Summons notices are prepared in triplicate: original kept, duplicate signed and returned, one copy left with suspect.
propositions.quote: The documentary evidence also notes the format and appearances of summons; it states that the notice is prepared in triplicate. The original is kept at the police station, the duplicate copy is signed, dated and returned by the suspect and one copy is left with the suspect.

propositions.text: The claimant's summons lacks signature or receipt acknowledgment, inconsistent with documentary evidence.
propositions.quote: The summons tendered by the claimant includes a section that is an acknowledgement that the summons was received; however this section has been left blank with no signature or acknowledgement of receipt by anybody. This is not consistent with the documentary evidence as noted above.

paragraphs.summary: Summonses are triplicated with signed receipt copies, but claimant's summons lacks signature, inconsistent with evidence.

propositions.text: A summons is issued to the named person or family member who must sign receipt.
propositions.quote: A summons is either issued to the person named in the summons or to a family or household member and the person who receives the summons is expected to sign in that regard.

propositions.text: The claimant's summons lacks his address, inconsistent with national documentation samples.
propositions.quote: I also note that the summons that was tendered did not identify the claimant's address on the face of the document, which is also not consistent with the sample in the document in the national documentation package.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes summonses require signature and address, but claimant's summons lacks address, inconsistent with samples.

propositions.text: Claimant's counsel argues summonses vary by PSB office.
propositions.quote: The claimant's counsel has submitted that there may be substantial differences in the type of information on summons' issued by PSB offices.

propositions.text: The court prefers independent China country documentation over claimant's counsel's argument on summons differences.
propositions.quote: However, I prefer the evidence of the China country documentation in regard to the issuance of summonses, as this information is provided by unbiased independent sources with no interest in the outcome of any particular refugee claim.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant's counsel argues summonses vary, but court prefers independent China documentation on summons issuance.

propositions.text: It is reasonable to expect a PSB summons to include the person's address for proper service.
propositions.quote: Further, it is reasonable to expect that a Public Security Bureau document would include the address of the person named on the summons since this information would be required by the serving officer to correctly identify the location of the individual's known address and to affect service of the document.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds a PSB summons should include the person's address for correct service.

propositions.text: The claimant's summons lacks a serial number, unlike samples in the National Documentation Package.
propositions.quote: In addition, upon further review of the document I note that there is no serial number on the face of the summons which also does not correspond with the sample contained in the National Documentation Package.

propositions.text: The summons has an official PSB seal, but handwriting over it undermines its purpose.
propositions.quote: I further note that the summons tendered by the claimant bears what appears to be an official seal of the Public Security Bureau. It is my belief that the purpose of the seal is to seal the document in order to demonstrate the document has not been altered or tampered with. However, the seal on this summons has handwriting which has been written over the seal thereby undermining the intended purpose of the seal.

propositions.text: Due to inconsistencies, the summons is given little weight by the court.
propositions.quote: On the basis of the inconsistencies in the summons provided by the claimant I can give little weight to this document.

paragraphs.summary: The summons lacks serial number and has handwriting over the seal; court gives it little weight due to inconsistencies.

propositions.text: The claimant used a smuggler to leave China and travel to Canada.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges that the claimant used the services of a smuggler to leave China and travel to Canada.

propositions.text: The claimant did not know the name, country, or type of passport used to travel with the smuggler.
propositions.quote: The claimant stated that the claimant only glanced at the passport and saw that his picture was in it but saw no other information. The claimant did not know the colour of the passport or which country issued the passport.

propositions.text: The claimant did not know the smuggler's travel name or passport details despite traveling together.
propositions.quote: The claimant also did not know what type of passport the smuggler was using or what name the smuggler was using to travel; despite the fact that the smuggler and the claimant were travelling together.

propositions.text: The claimant's lack of knowledge about travel documents is not excused by vulnerability or smuggler instructions.
propositions.quote: While I do recognize the need for the board to be sensitive to the vulnerabilities of claimants travelling under false documents I do not find that it excuses the claimant for his testimonial failings concerning the lack of knowledge of the identity he was travelling under.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant used a smuggler but lacked knowledge of travel documents; court finds this lack of knowledge not excused.

propositions.text: The claimant's claim of following smuggler instructions does not explain his ignorance of travel identities.
propositions.quote: The fact that the claimant claimed to be following instructions of the smuggler does not explain why he could not relate anything of significance about the identities he and the smuggler were travelling under.

propositions.text: It is not plausible or credible that the claimant was unaware of basic travel identity information despite likely questioning.
propositions.quote: I find it neither plausible nor credible that the claimant would not be aware of this basic information in the face of the obvious likelihood that he would be questioned about it in transit.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it not credible that the claimant was unaware of travel identities despite smuggler instructions.

propositions.text: The claimant testified that all bibles were seized during the church raid by the PSB.
propositions.quote: The claimant testified that during the raid of the underground house church all of the bibles were seized by the Public Security Bureau.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence states the PSB issues receipts for seized items during investigations.
propositions.quote: Documentary evidence states that the Public Security Bureau will issue a receipt for items that are seized in the course of an investigation.

propositions.text: The claimant testified no receipts were issued for the seized bibles.
propositions.quote: The claimant was questioned with respect to the issuance of receipts by the PSB and the claimant's testimony was that there were no receipts.

propositions.text: Since the PSB issued a summons to the claimant, they appear to follow the rule of law.
propositions.quote: Given that the Public Security Bureau has allegedly issued a summons to the claimant it would appear that in the claimant's case they are not averse to following the rule of law.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant says bibles were seized without receipts, but PSB usually issues receipts and issued a summons, showing rule of law compliance.

propositions.text: It is reasonable to expect a receipt for seized bibles if the raid occurred.
propositions.quote: As such it is reasonable to expect that a receipt would have been issued for the seizure or confiscation of bibles at the time of the raid if it had occurred.

propositions.text: A negative inference is drawn from the lack of receipt, leading to finding claimant not pursued by PSB as alleged.
propositions.quote: I draw a negative inference from the lack of receipt issued for the confiscation of bibles. Based on the foregoing findings and negative inferences I find on a balance of probabilities that the claimant is not being pursued by the Public Security Bureau as he has alleged.

paragraphs.summary: The court draws a negative inference from no receipt for seized bibles and finds claimant not pursued by PSB as alleged.

propositions.text: The claimant alleges he became involved in Christianity in 2009 but only believed after one month with the preachers.
propositions.quote: With respect to the claimant's identity as a Christian, the claimant alleges that he became involved in Christianity in XXXX 2009 but did not believe in Christianity until one month after meeting the preachers from Taiwan.

propositions.text: The church was raided about a month after he became a Christian.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges that the church was raided approximately a month after he became a Christian.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges involvement in Christianity in 2009, belief after one month, and church raid about a month later.

propositions.text: The claimant answered most religious questions but lacked understanding of absolution of sin related to Jesus' death.
propositions.quote: The claimant was asked a number of questions concerning his religious knowledge. While the claimant was able to answer most questions it was clear that he did not have a clear understanding of the concept of absolution of sin as it relates to the crucifixion and death of Jesus.

propositions.text: Christians believe absolution of original sin comes only through baptism.
propositions.quote: Christians believe that the absolution of original sin only comes through baptism.

propositions.text: It is reasonable to expect the claimant to know the distinction about absolution of sin; a negative inference is drawn.
propositions.quote: It is reasonable to expect that the claimant would know this distinction. In this regard I draw a negative inference.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant lacked understanding of Christian absolution of sin; court draws a negative inference on this knowledge gap.

propositions.text: Claimant's knowledge of Christianity does not prove he is a genuine practicing Christian.
propositions.quote: While the claimant was able to demonstrate some knowledge of Christianity that knowledge does not necessarily mean that the claimant is a genuine practicing Christian.

propositions.text: The claimant produced a baptismal certificate and two letters from Reverend XX indicating church attendance since 2009.
propositions.quote: The claimant produced a baptismal certificate and two letters from Reverend XX The letters indicate that the claimant has been attending church in Canada since XXXX of 2009.

propositions.text: The letters attest to participation but not motivation; recent case law says pastor's faith assessment cannot substitute panel's assessment.
propositions.quote: These documents can only attest to the claimant's participation in church activities, they do not attest to his motivation. In this regard recent case law indicates that a pastor's assessment on the genuineness of a person's faith can not be substituted for the assessment the panel is required to make.

propositions.text: Little weight is given to Reverend XX's letter in assessing claimant's Christian faith genuineness.
propositions.quote: Given the foregoing I give little weight to the letter from Reverend XX in assessing the genuineness of the claimant's Christian faith.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant's documents show church attendance but not faith genuineness; court gives little weight to pastor's letter.

propositions.text: It is difficult but necessary to judge the genuineness of religious practice in this case.
propositions.quote: While it is difficult to make a judgment regarding the genuineness of a person's religious practice, it is necessary in this case.

propositions.text: Considering all evidence and prior untrustworthy testimony, claimant was not a Christian in China.
propositions.quote: In doing so I have considered the totality of the evidence available, having previously found that the claimant's testimony concerning the claimant's alleged house church in China untrustworthy, I further find on a balance of probabilities that the claimant was not a Christian in China.

propositions.text: Claimant's allegation of practicing Christianity in China is not credible and was made to support a fraudulent claim.
propositions.quote: I further find that the claimant's allegation that he was a practicing Christian in China is not credible and was only made for the purpose of supporting a fraudulent claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant was not a Christian in China and his claim was not credible but fraudulent.

propositions.text: Having found claimant was not Christian in China, court must consider if claimant is genuine Christian in Canada.
propositions.quote: Having found that you were not a Christian in China I must consider whether you are a genuine practicing Christian in this country.

propositions.text: There is a good faith requirement in making a refugee claim to prevent unilateral determination of refugee status in sur place cases.
propositions.quote: There is a requirement for good faith in making a refugee claim. In this regard, R.P.G. Haines, the Chairman of a refugee status appeal panel and A.G. Wang Heed, a member of the United Nations High Commission for Refugees stated in part: If there is no good faith requirement in the sur place situation, it places in the hands of the appellant for refugee status the means of unilaterally determining the grant to him or her of refugee status.

paragraphs.summary: The court must consider if claimant is genuine Christian in Canada and notes good faith is required in refugee claims.

propositions.text: An individual who manipulates circumstances to create a real chance of persecution cannot be said to belong to 'sur place' claim category.
propositions.quote: An individual who as a stratagem deliberately manipulates circumstances to create a real chance of persecution, which did not exist, cannot be said to belong to this category.

propositions.text: The claim has not been made in good faith on a balance of probabilities and context of findings and negative inferences.
propositions.quote: the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, and in the context of all of the findings and negative inferences drawn above, that this claim has not been made in good faith.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds the claim was not made in good faith and cites Hathaway on 'sur place' claims manipulation (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: Claimant is not a genuine practicing Christian in China and joined a Canadian church to support a fraudulent refugee claim.
propositions.quote: the claimant joined a Christian church in Canada only for the purpose of supporting a fraudulent refugee claim.

propositions.text: Claimant is not a genuine practicing Christian nor perceived as such in China based on totality of evidence and Christian knowledge.
propositions.quote: the claimant is not a genuine practicing Christian nor would he be perceived to be in China.

paragraphs.summary: Panel finds claimant not a genuine Christian and joined Canadian church to support fraudulent claim (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: Whether claimant faces serious possibility of persecution if returning to China to practice Christianity in unregistered church.
propositions.quote: the panel has considered whether there is a serious possibility that the claimant would be persecuted if he returns to China and chooses to practice Christianity in an unregistered church.

propositions.text: Claimant is from Fujian province; evidence suggests Fujian and Guangdong have most liberal religious policy in China.
propositions.quote: The claimant is from Fujian province. The panel notes the documentary evidence suggests by virtue of the absence of evidence of incidents of persecution that Fujian and Guangdong have the most liberal policy on religion in China.

propositions.text: Chinese authorities show high tolerance to Christian activities, especially non-registered groups, per Hong Kong Christian Council 2010.
propositions.quote: The Executive Secretary of the Hong Kong Christian Council recently stated in XXXX, 2010 correspondence that the Chinese authorities have demonstrated a high degree of tolerance to Christian activities in general and particularly towards non-registered groups.

paragraphs.summary: Panel considers risk of persecution in Fujian; evidence shows liberal religious policy and tolerance to non-registered Christian groups (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: No documented arrests of Christians in Fujian province from 2005 to 2010 despite arrests elsewhere in China.
propositions.quote: none of these arrests were noted as being in Fujian province.

propositions.text: Multiple provinces had house church crackdowns and arrests, but Fujian province had none documented.
propositions.quote: there have been no such arrests in Fujian province. Documentary evidence submitted does not provide any recent evidence of arrests of Christians in Fujian province.

paragraphs.summary: No documented arrests of Christians in Fujian province from 2005-2010, unlike other provinces (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: 2009 report shows arrests and persecution of Christians in China but none in Fujian province.
propositions.quote: no arrests occurred in Fujian province where the claimant is from.

propositions.text: Panel finds no evidence of recent arrests of Christians in Fujian province after reviewing documentary evidence.
propositions.quote: The panel has reviewed all the documentary evidence submitted and finds no evidence of recent arrests of Christians in Fujian province.

paragraphs.summary: Panel finds no evidence of recent Christian arrests in Fujian province per 2009 report and documentary evidence (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: China Aid Association 2010 report notes 10 persons persecuted in Fujian, with one church venue closed and one staffer detained.
propositions.quote: The China Aid Association's (CAA) 2010 annual report states that ten persons were persecuted in Fujian province in 2010... one church staffer was detained.

propositions.text: Report lacks details on persecution nature and church registration status; panel gives it little weight for risk assessment.
propositions.quote: As such, the panel can give the report little weight in assessing the over risk of persecution of Christians in Fujian.

propositions.text: No information in report that persons were arrested or sentenced for underground church activities.
propositions.quote: there is no information in the report that persons were arrested or sentenced for underground church activities.

paragraphs.summary: CAA 2010 report notes some persecution in Fujian but lacks details; panel gives it little weight and finds no arrests for underground church activities (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: If recent arrests of Christians in Fujian had occurred, there would be documentation; none found on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that if there were recent arrests of Christians in Fujian province, there would be some documentation of these arrests.

paragraphs.summary: Panel finds no recent Christian arrests in Fujian likely given lack of documentation (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: Maldonado principle: claimant's sworn allegations presumed true unless rebutted by reasons to doubt truthfulness.
propositions.quote: when a refugee claimant swears to the truth of certain allegations, a presumption is created that those allegations are true unless there are reasons to doubt their truthfulness.

propositions.text: Presumption of truthfulness is rebuttable, including by documentary evidence failing to mention expected facts.
propositions.quote: the presumption that a claimant's own testimony is true is always rebuttable and, in appropriate circumstances, may be rebutted by the failure of the documentary evidence to mention what one would normally expect it to mention.

paragraphs.summary: Maldonado principle presumes claimant's sworn allegations true but presumption is rebuttable by documentary evidence (prior court or authority).

propositions.text: Claimant testified all 18 members were arrested, detained six months, fined, and two leaders deported.
propositions.quote: The claimant testified that all 18 members were arrested and detained for six months and fined and the two leaders of the church were deported.

propositions.text: Many observers report religious persecution in China, including underground Christian house churches in remote areas.
propositions.quote: There are a number of observers... who strive to inform the world that religious persecution takes place in China.

propositions.text: Egregious incident alleged by claimant would be expected to be reported but is not documented.
propositions.quote: One would expect that and an egregious incident such as alleged by the claimant would be reported.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant alleges arrests and deportations; panel notes such egregious incidents would be reported but are not documented (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: Justice Crampton found it reasonable to conclude persecution of underground Christians in Fujian would be documented if it existed.
propositions.quote: it was reasonable for the panel to find that, if underground Christians faced a serious possibility of persecution in Fujian Province, it would have been documented.

propositions.text: Panel was not unreasonable to differentiate treatment of Catholics and underground Protestants in Fujian.
propositions.quote: the panel was not unreasonable to differentiate between the treatment of Catholics and underground Protestants in Fujian.

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court decision supports panel's view that persecution in Fujian would be documented and treatment differs between Catholics and underground Protestants (prior court or authority).

propositions.text: China Aid Association admits not all persecution cases documented in every province including Fujian and Guangdong.
propositions.quote: China Aid Association (CAA) has stated... they have not documented all cases of persecution and religious repression occurring in every province in China, including Guangdong and Fujian.

propositions.text: No mention of recent arrests of lay Christians in Fujian in any documentation on religious persecution in China.
propositions.quote: there has been no mention at all of recent arrests of lay Christians in Fujian province in any of the documentation regarding religious persecution in China

propositions.text: US report notes religious freedom varies widely; unregistered groups expanded and operate openly in many regions.
propositions.quote: the extent of religious freedom in China continues to vary widely within the country... most Christian groups... no longer operate in strict secrecy... carried out public activities...

propositions.text: Situation in Fujian does not reflect provinces with arrests of ordinary Christians; government supervision minimal in some regions.
propositions.quote: The panel finds that the situation in Fujian province does not reflect what is happening in many other provinces where there have been arrests of ordinary Christians.

paragraphs.summary: Panel notes CAA admits incomplete documentation; no recent arrests in Fujian; religious freedom varies widely; Fujian situation is more tolerant (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: British Home Office report states 50-70 million Protestants practice without state sanction; 20 million in state-approved churches.
propositions.quote: there are fifty to seventy million Protestant Christians in China who practice without state sanction and that only twenty million practice their religion in state approved churches.

propositions.text: Prayer meetings and Bible study groups among friends and families need not register with authorities.
propositions.quote: prayer meetings and Bible study groups held among friends and families need not register with authorities.

paragraphs.summary: British Home Office reports many Protestants practice without state sanction; informal groups need not register (prior court or authority).

propositions.text: Risk of persecution for practicing Christians in Fujian is low per supporting documentary evidence.
propositions.quote: the supporting documentary evidence for the claimant's home province of Fujian indicates, the risk of persecution for practicing Christians is low.

propositions.text: Even if harm qualifies as serious, panel must consider if serious possibility harm will occur; laws alone insufficient.
propositions.quote: the panel must consider whether there is a serious possibility that the harm will actually come to pass... A statute... may provide for unconscionably severe punishment... but this does not necessarily mean there is a serious possibility that the punishment will be inflicted.

propositions.text: Supreme Court emphasizes considering laws and their application in assessing objective well-founded fear, citing UNHCR Handbook.
propositions.quote: The Supreme Court has emphasized that... relevant factors include the laws in the claimant's homeland, together with the manner in which they are applied... cited paragraph 43 of the UNHCR Handbook.

paragraphs.summary: Panel finds low risk of persecution in Fujian; must consider likelihood of harm, not just laws; Supreme Court guidance cited (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: Claimant is free to worship in any Christian congregation in Fujian province if returned.
propositions.quote: the claimant is free to choose to worship in the Christian congregation of her choosing.

propositions.text: Panel relies on reliable, probative documentary evidence from reputable independent sources about Christian situation in Fujian.
propositions.quote: The panel has chosen to rely on the documentary evidence because it originates from a variety of reputable independent sources...

paragraphs.summary: Panel concludes claimant free to worship in Fujian and relies on reliable documentary evidence from reputable sources (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, claimant would be able to practice religion in any church in Fujian without serious risk of persecution.
propositions.quote: The panel has considered the documentary evidence and the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant would be able to practice his religion in any church in Fujian province... and that there is not a serious possibility that he would be persecuted for doing so.

paragraphs.summary: Panel finds claimant can practice religion in Fujian without serious risk of persecution (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: Justice Russell decision supports panel's finding on Fujian's religious policies and lack of documented persecution.
propositions.quote: While this decision concerns an alleged raid in Guangdong Province, the profile of Fujian province is virtually identical...

propositions.text: Justice Crampton found it reasonable to conclude persecution in Fujian would be documented if it occurred.
propositions.quote: it was reasonable for the Board to conclude that if persecution of members of underground churches occurred in Fujian province it would have been documented.

propositions.text: Justice Lemieux noted documentary evidence indicates minimal constraints on religious practice in Fujian and general freedom.
propositions.quote: the documentary evidence concerning Fujian province indicates there is a minimum of constraints on religious practice and people generally practice their religion freely.

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court decisions by Justices Russell, Crampton, and Lemieux support panel's findings on Fujian's religious freedom and lack of persecution documentation (prior court or authority).

propositions.text: Justice Zinn noted claimant's testimony on alleged raid was questioned by documentary evidence leading to inference raid did not occur.
propositions.quote: there was documentary evidence before the Board that brought his evidence of the raid into question and lead to an inference that no such raid occurred.

paragraphs.summary: Justice Zinn found documentary evidence questioned claimant's testimony on raid, inferring no raid occurred (prior court or authority).

propositions.text: Justice O'Keefe held Board's finding that Christians may practice freely in Fujian province is reasonable.
propositions.quote: this Court has held on several occasions that the Board's finding that Christian may practice freely in Fujian province is reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Justice O'Keefe affirmed Board's reasonable finding that Christians may practice freely in Fujian (prior court or authority).

propositions.text: Claimant has not met burden to establish serious possibility of persecution or risk of cruel treatment or torture in China.
propositions.quote: the panel finds that the claimant has not satisfied his burden of establishing a serious possibility that he would be persecuted or that he would be personally subjected to a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture by any authority in the People's Republic of China.

paragraphs.summary: Panel concludes claimant failed to prove serious possibility of persecution or risk of cruel treatment or torture in China (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: Refugee Protection Division rejects claimant's refugee claim.
propositions.quote: The Refugee Protection Division therefore rejects his claim.

paragraphs.summary: Refugee Protection Division rejects claimant's refugee claim (earlier decision-maker).
